title: Progressive Fidelity and SDK Flow Patterns - Hosted API PRD (draft)
content:
Summary

This PRD sketches a combined approach for progressive fidelity streaming, deterministic tool invocation semantics, and SDK ergonomics aimed at low-latency conversational integrations. The objective is to let product teams trade off speed, cost, and structured reliability in a predictable way while keeping the client surface ergonomic across web, server, and mobile clients. This is purposefully a working draft with a number of open questions and suggested experiments.

Motivation and problems we see in the wild
- Customers want faster perceived response times than bulk generation provides. They also need reliable structured outputs for downstream tools and databases.
- Tool calling today is brittle when models stream partial answers and clients attempt to invoke side effects early.
- SDKs either hide too much (opaque stream) or demand complex client-side orchestration for retries and resumability.

High level proposal
1) Progressive fidelity streaming: responses emitted in labeled fidelity tiers (hint, candidate, final). Each chunk includes a lightweight fidelity header, optional partial structured fragment, and an idempotency token. This enables clients to display early content while deferring tool invocation until a confidence threshold or final chunk.
2) Tool invocation contract: explicit lifecycle for tool calls - propose, confirm, execute, ack. Tool calls may be emitted optimistically but include a proposed execution token and an explicit confirm operation from the client when safe. Server records and exposes tool-call id + idempotency metadata.
3) SDK flow primitives: high-level client APIs that expose async iterators for streams, a small backpressure API for mobile, and typed helpers for structured output parsing and validation. Provide both low-level stream event hooks and higher-level conversation objects for quick adoption.

Goals (success metrics)
- Perceived first-word latency reduced by 30% for targeted workloads where progressive fidelity is enabled.
- Tool-invocation misfires (unintended side effects) reduced by 90% when confirm semantics are enabled.
- SDK adoption: 60% of new integrations use the streaming async iterator pattern within 6 months of launch.
- Error rate and ambiguity for structured outputs dropped measurably on customer eval prompt sets.

Non goals
- This PRD does not cover orchestration for multi-model fusions (that is a separate initiative).
- Not proposing new model training; this is API and SDK surface design only.

Core UX and API surfaces
1) Streaming envelope and fidelity labels
- Each stream delta is framed as a JSON-lite envelope (server-sent-event friendly) consisting of: chunk_id, fidelity_level, seq_no, partial_text (optional), partial_structured (optional), token_cost_estimate (optional), ttfb_ms (optional), provenance_hint (model variant).
- Fidelity levels: hint, candidate, final. hint = very early, high hallucination risk; candidate = plausible draft; final = quality-gated output.
- Clients may display hint and candidate but should only invoke tools on candidate+ if confirm policy allows.

2) Structured partial fragments and schema evolution
- Partial_structured is an incremental JSON fragment that conforms to a declared schema version id. The server guarantees that merging ordered partial fragments yields a JSON instance that validates against the schema when the stream ends with final fidelity.
- Support for optional schema_version header and a fallback parsing strategy when unknown versions are encountered. SDK exposes a strict parser and a permissive parser option.

3) Tool lifecycle and idempotency
- Tool propose: model emits a tool_propose event containing tool_id, args_preview (redacted), proposed_execution_token, and estimated_effect_description. This is non-binding.
- Client confirm: client issues a confirm_tool_call API with proposed_execution_token and optional conditions (e.g., stable_text_hash, user_consent).
- Execute: once confirmed, server attempts execution and emits tool_exec_result in the stream. Execution receives a canonical execution_id and idempotency metadata.
- Abort and fallback: if execution fails or confirm timeout elapses, server emits a fallback_candidate at candidate fidelity.

4) Backpressure, resumption, and session semantics
- Clients can signal backpressure with a per-connection credit token. Server will not emit new candidate chunks beyond credits. Credits can be increased incrementally. Useful for mobile and low-memory environments.
- Streams are resumable with stable session_id and last_seq_no. SDK should provide a resume method that requests missing chunks or asks for a succinct re-run from a checkpoint.

SDK ergonomic surface proposals (recommended defaults)
- High level: Conversation client - conversation.start(), conversation.next_chunk() async iterator, conversation.confirm_tool(proposed_token), conversation.resume(checkpoint). This is the recommended path for most apps.
- Mid level: Stream observer - on_chunk(fn), request(n) backpressure API, on_tool_propose(fn) hook, confirmTool(token). Good for specialized apps that want granular control.
- Low level: Raw SSE/WS frames for power users. Include a helper to materialize partial_structured fragments into full JSON with validation.
- Language SDKs: JS/TS, Python first. Native mobile: thin wrappers around the async iterator with built-in backpressure heuristics and small persistent checkpoint stores.

Examples and patterns
- Pattern A: Fast chat UI. Display hint immediately with a subtle shimmer. When candidate with confidence >= threshold arrives, show stable text and present in-UI tool actions. If tool_propose is presented, show a confirm button bound to the confirm_tool endpoint to avoid accidental side effects.
- Pattern B: Command palette. Accept candidate text suggestions but require explicit user keystroke to confirm tool execution. For automated flows, use confirm_tool with additional verification like stable_text_hash.
- Pattern C: Database write pipelines. Use final fidelity only for writes by default. Optionally enable confirm on candidate if downstream compensating transactions are supported.

Rollout plan and experiments
- Phase 0 (internal): implement fidelity labels and streaming envelope, add SDK hooks. Build e2e prototype with the playground and instrument metrics. Duration 6 weeks.
- Phase 1 (beta customers): enable proposed API for 3 pilot customers. Run canary with kill switch and monitor tool-invocation misfires, latency distribution, and resume success rates. Duration 8 weeks.
- Phase 2 (general availability): default SDKs shipped, documentation, migration guide, and telemetry dashboards.

Telemetry and observability
- Key metrics to collect: first-chunk latency, candidate-to-final delta, tool-propose counts, confirm latency, tool-exec success rate, resume success rate, schema validation failures, partial_fragment_reassembly_errors.
- Traceability: stream chunks and tool lifecycle include stable ids surfaceable in Console trace views. Provide per-route breakdowns and per-model variant profiles.

Security, privacy and compliance notes
- Tool proposals and args_preview must be redacted by default. Allow customer-controlled exposure flags for sensitive internal tools only with enterprise agreements.
- Execution audit logs: all confirmed tool calls produce a tamper-evident audit entry accessible via Private/ Dedicated control planes.

Open questions and tradeoffs
- How to set confidence metrics for fidelity transitions. Propose a lightweight score but models need to expose calibrated probability estimates or we rely on model heuristics.
- Amount of state kept for resumability. Full KV checkpointing is expensive; suggest periodic checkpoints and event-driven delta replay.
- UX complexity for clients. We need to balance power vs simplicity. Consider shipping both a high-level Conversation client and an optional low-level stream API.

Appendix A - Quick API sketches
- POST /v1/conversation/streams - starts a streaming session, returns session_id and an SSE stream. Body includes desired schema_version, max_fidelity_hint, and backpressure_credit.
- POST /v1/tool/confirm - confirm a proposed tool invocation. Body: { proposed_token, session_id, conditions } -> returns execution_id or error.

Appendix B - Migration guidelines for existing SDK users
- Default behavior remains unchanged until customers opt in to progressive_fidelity flag.
- Provide a transpiler utility to convert older callbacks to the new async iterator pattern for backwards compatibility.

Notes to self and TODOs
- Sync with applied-ml on how to surface fidelity calibration signals from model scoring. Action: schedule runbook with Priya.
- Design the streaming envelope wire format for minimal overhead for mobile. See infra note: wire format must be <= 40 bytes overhead per small chunk.
- Create a confluence page with sample UI patterns and code snippets for web/mobile.

References and links
- Related tickets: JIRA:API-842, LIN:RED-204.
- Early prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-api/pull/612

End of draft

(If you are reading this and have a hard opinion about fidelity names, backpressure semantics, or tool confirm flows please add inline comments or ping in #product-hosted-api)
